notes.definition: Scientists and concerned citizens have put in place programmes to reduce the negative effects of humans on ecosystems and biodiversity, such as breeding programmes, protecting rare habitats, replanting hedgerows and field margins, reducing deforestation and carbon dioxide emissions, and recycling.
explanation: Human activities have both negative and positive effects on ecosystems. Negative interactions include deforestation, pollution, destroying habitats for building, quarrying and farming, and releasing greenhouse gases. Positive interactions are the deliberate actions people take to protect species and habitats. Scientists and concerned citizens have put in place programmes to reduce the negative effects of humans on ecosystems and biodiversity. The AQA specification names five types of programme.

Breeding programmes for endangered species: zoos and conservation centres breed animals and plants that are at risk of extinction, keeping a population alive in captivity and maintaining genetic variety by carefully choosing which individuals breed. Some offspring can be released back into the wild once their habitat is safe. Protection and regeneration of rare habitats: areas such as coral reefs, mangroves, peat bogs and heathland can be protected as nature reserves or marine protected areas, and damaged habitats can be restored, for example by replanting native species or rewetting drained bogs.

Reintroduction of field margins and hedgerows: in agricultural areas where farmers grow only one type of crop (monoculture), biodiversity is very low. Many hedgerows were removed in the past to make larger fields for machinery. Replanting hedgerows and leaving wide strips of wild plants (field margins) around crops provides food, shelter and nesting sites for many species of insects, birds and mammals, and acts as a corridor so animals can move between habitats. Pollinating insects and predators of crop pests can also benefit farmers.

Reduction of deforestation and carbon dioxide emissions by some governments: some countries have laws or agreements to limit forest clearance, protect forest reserves or replant trees, and to reduce carbon dioxide emissions by using renewable energy. This protects habitats directly and reduces global warming. Recycling resources rather than dumping waste in landfill reduces the land used for landfill, reduces pollution and reduces the need to extract new raw materials (for example by quarrying or mining), which protects habitats.

Maintaining biodiversity often involves conflicting pressures. Protecting a forest may stop local people earning money from farming or logging; leaving field margins means a farmer has less land for crops; breeding programmes and nature reserves cost money; and reducing carbon dioxide emissions can increase energy costs. In the exam you may be given information and asked to evaluate these pressures. A good answer considers the benefits for biodiversity, the costs to people (economic and social), and possible compromises, and then reaches a justified conclusion.
keyFacts: Programmes to maintain biodiversity are run by scientists and concerned citizens.
Breeding programmes help to protect endangered species.
Rare habitats can be protected and regenerated.
Field margins and hedgerows are reintroduced in areas of monoculture farming.
Some governments are reducing deforestation and carbon dioxide emissions.
Recycling resources rather than dumping waste in landfill helps biodiversity.
Human interactions with ecosystems can be positive or negative.
There are conflicting pressures (economic, social and environmental) on maintaining biodiversity.

keyTerms.definition: A species at risk of becoming extinct because its population is very small or falling quickly.
A planned scheme, often in zoos, to breed endangered species in captivity to increase their numbers, sometimes releasing them into the wild.
A line of shrubs and small trees planted along the edge of a field.
A strip of land around the edge of a crop field left with wild flowers and grasses, not sprayed or ploughed.
Growing only one type of crop over a large area.
Restoring a damaged habitat, for example by replanting native species or rewetting a drained bog.
The protection and careful management of species and habitats to maintain biodiversity.

equations.name: Percentage change
equations.formula: percentage change = (new value − original value) ÷ original value × 100

workedExamples.title: Effect of field margins on bees
workedExamples.question: Use the bar chart in the notes. Calculate the percentage increase in the number of bee species between fields with no margin and fields with a 6 m margin.
steps: No margin = 8 bee species; 6 m margin = 26 bee species.

workedExamples.title: Growth of a captive-bred population
workedExamples.question: A breeding programme began with 22 individuals of an endangered bird. After 15 years there were 154 birds. Calculate how many times larger the population became, and the percentage increase.
steps: 154 ÷ 22 = 7, so the population became 7 times larger.

workedExamples.title: Evaluating a conflict
workedExamples.question: A farmer is offered a payment to leave a 6 m field margin around a wheat field. Give one advantage and one disadvantage for the farmer.
steps: Advantage: more pollinators and natural predators of pests may live in the margin, which can help crops; the farmer receives a payment.
Disadvantage: less land is available to grow wheat, so the yield and income from the field fall.
A conclusion depends on whether the payment and pest control benefits outweigh the lost crop.
workedExamples.answer: Advantage: payment and more pollinators or pest predators. Disadvantage: less land for crops.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that breeding programmes alone can save a species.
misconceptions.right: In fact, released animals need a safe habitat, so breeding programmes work best alongside habitat protection and regeneration.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all human interactions with ecosystems are negative.
misconceptions.right: In fact, humans also have positive effects, such as conservation programmes, replanting hedgerows and protecting habitats.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think recycling has nothing to do with biodiversity.
misconceptions.right: In fact, recycling reduces landfill, pollution and the need to extract new raw materials, all of which protects habitats.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think maintaining biodiversity has no costs.
misconceptions.right: In fact, there are conflicting pressures: conservation can reduce farmers' yields, cost money and affect jobs, so decisions involve balancing benefits and costs.

realWorld: Zoos run coordinated breeding programmes for endangered animals such as snow leopards, and some species, such as the Arabian oryx, have been returned to the wild after captive breeding.
UK farmers can receive government payments for planting hedgerows and leaving wildflower margins around fields.
Marine protected areas restrict fishing so that fish populations and seabed habitats can recover.
International agreements commit many countries to reduce carbon dioxide emissions and to slow deforestation.
examTips: Learn the five programmes in the specification: breeding programmes, protecting and regenerating rare habitats, field margins and hedgerows, reducing deforestation and CO₂ emissions, and recycling.
For each method, explain how it increases or maintains biodiversity (for example 'provides food and shelter for more species').
In 'evaluate' questions, give benefits for biodiversity, costs or problems (money, jobs, lost farmland), and a justified conclusion.
Use data from the question: quote numbers and calculate changes to support your points.
Remember that field margins and hedgerows are linked to areas where farmers grow only one type of crop.
summary: Programmes reduce the negative effects of humans on ecosystems and biodiversity.
Rare habitats are protected and regenerated.
Field margins and hedgerows are reintroduced around monoculture crops.
Some governments reduce deforestation and carbon dioxide emissions.
Recycling instead of landfill reduces habitat loss and pollution.
Maintaining biodiversity involves conflicting pressures that must be evaluated.

flashcards.front: Name the five programmes AQA lists for maintaining biodiversity.
flashcards.back: Breeding programmes; protecting and regenerating rare habitats; field margins and hedgerows; reducing deforestation and CO₂ emissions; recycling instead of landfill.
Breeding endangered species in captivity to increase numbers, sometimes releasing them into the wild.

flashcards.front: Why are hedgerows and field margins reintroduced?
flashcards.back: In monoculture farmland they provide food, shelter and nesting sites, increasing biodiversity.
A strip of wild flowers and grasses left around a crop field, not sprayed or ploughed.
Less landfill, less pollution and less need to extract new raw materials, so fewer habitats are destroyed.

flashcards.front: Give an example of habitat regeneration.
flashcards.back: For example rewetting a drained peat bog or replanting native trees.

flashcards.front: Why do some governments reduce deforestation and CO₂ emissions?
flashcards.back: To protect habitats and reduce global warming, which both maintain biodiversity.

flashcards.front: Give one negative human interaction with ecosystems.
flashcards.back: For example deforestation, pollution or destroying habitats for building.

flashcards.front: Give one positive human interaction with ecosystems.
flashcards.back: For example breeding programmes, protecting habitats or planting hedgerows.

flashcards.front: Give one conflicting pressure on maintaining biodiversity.
flashcards.back: For example farmers lose land for crops, conservation costs money, or protecting forest limits jobs and income.

flashcards.front: Why must breeding programmes be linked to habitat protection?
flashcards.back: Released animals need a safe, suitable habitat to survive.

flashcards.front: Why do farmers sometimes remove hedgerows?
flashcards.back: To make bigger fields for machinery and more land for crops.

questions.question: Which of these is a programme to maintain biodiversity?
options: Removing hedgerows to make larger fields
markScheme: 1 mark: breeding programmes for endangered species
questions.explanation: Breeding programmes help endangered species. The other three reduce biodiversity.

questions.question: Why are hedgerows being replanted around fields?
options: To provide habitats, food and shelter for many species
To increase the use of pesticides
markScheme: 1 mark: to provide habitats, food and shelter
questions.explanation: Hedgerows support insects, birds and mammals, increasing biodiversity in farmland. Replanting them makes fields smaller, not larger.

questions.question: Which of these helps to maintain biodiversity by reducing the need for landfill?
markScheme: 1 mark: recycling
questions.explanation: Recycling resources rather than dumping them in landfill reduces habitat loss and pollution.

questions.question: In which type of farming area are field margins and hedgerows most useful for increasing biodiversity?
options: Where many different crops grow in small fields
Where farmers grow only one type of crop
markScheme: 1 mark: where farmers grow only one type of crop
questions.explanation: Monocultures have very low biodiversity, so adding margins and hedgerows makes a big difference.

questions.question: Which is an example of protecting and regenerating a rare habitat?
options: Rewetting a drained peat bog and replanting Sphagnum moss
markScheme: 1 mark: rewetting a drained peat bog and replanting moss
questions.explanation: Regeneration restores damaged habitats. The other options damage habitats.

questions.question: Why do zoos carefully choose which animals breed in a breeding programme?
options: To maintain genetic variety in the population
markScheme: 1 mark: to maintain genetic variety
questions.explanation: Choosing unrelated parents keeps genetic variety, which helps the population survive changes such as disease.

questions.question: How can government action to reduce carbon dioxide emissions help maintain biodiversity?
options: It reduces global warming, so fewer habitats are lost and fewer species change distribution
It increases the amount of landfill
markScheme: 1 mark: reduces global warming, so fewer habitats are lost
questions.explanation: Lower carbon dioxide emissions slow global warming, which reduces loss of habitats and changes to species distribution.

questions.question: A government protects a large forest from logging. Which is a conflicting pressure that might arise?
options: More carbon dioxide is absorbed by trees
Local people lose jobs and income from logging
markScheme: 1 mark: local people lose jobs and income
questions.explanation: The other options are benefits of protection. Loss of jobs and income is a cost that conflicts with conservation.

questions.question: Use the bar chart in the notes. Which statement is best supported by the data?
options: Field margins reduce the number of bee species
Field margins have no effect on plant species
Wider field margins are associated with more bee and plant species
Only bees benefit from field margins
markScheme: 1 mark: wider margins are associated with more bee and plant species
questions.explanation: Both bee species (8, 19, 26) and plant species (14, 27, 35) increase as margin width increases. 'Associated with' is the correct cautious wording for survey data.

questions.question: Use the bar chart in the notes. How many more plant species were found in fields with a 6 m margin than in fields with no margin?
questions.explanation: The 6 m margin had 35 plant species and no margin had 14, so there were 21 more.

questions.question: Use the bar chart in the notes. Calculate the percentage increase in the number of plant species from fields with no margin to fields with a 3 m margin. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
questions.explanation: 13 ÷ 14 = 0.929, which is 93% to the nearest whole number.

questions.question: A breeding programme started with 40 animals. After 10 years there were 130. Calculate the percentage increase in the population.
questions.explanation: The population increased by 90. 90 ÷ 40 = 2.25, so the increase is 225%.

questions.question: A farm had 12.5 km of hedgerows in 1990. By 2020, after replanting, it had 16 km. Calculate the percentage increase in the length of hedgerow.
questions.explanation: The hedgerow increased by 3.5 km. 3.5 ÷ 12.5 = 0.28, a 28% increase.

questions.question: A farmer has a square field with sides of 200 m. She leaves a field margin 6 m wide around all four edges. Calculate the percentage of the field's area that is now used for the margin. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
markScheme: 1 mark: crop area = 188 × 188 = 35 344 m², so margin area = 40 000 − 35 344 = 4656 m²
questions.explanation: The cropped area is a square of side 200 − 2 × 6 = 188 m. Margin area = 40 000 − 35 344 = 4656 m², which is 11.6% of the field. This shows the cost to the farmer of leaving a margin.

questions.question: A council recycled 34% of its 90 000 tonnes of waste in 2015. In 2022 it recycled 52% of 85 000 tonnes. Calculate how many more tonnes were recycled in 2022 than in 2015.
questions.explanation: Work out the mass recycled each year first, then subtract. You cannot just subtract the percentages because the total waste was different each year.

questions.question: Give two programmes that have been put in place to maintain biodiversity.
markScheme: 1 mark each, up to 2: breeding programmes for endangered species; protection and regeneration of rare habitats; reintroducing field margins and hedgerows; reducing deforestation and carbon dioxide emissions; recycling rather than landfill
questions.explanation: These five programmes are named in the AQA specification.

questions.question: State what is meant by an endangered species.
markScheme: 1 mark: a species at risk of becoming extinct
questions.explanation: Endangered species have small or rapidly falling populations.

questions.question: Explain how replanting hedgerows can increase biodiversity on farmland.
markScheme: 1 mark: hedgerows provide food, shelter or nesting sites (habitats)
1 mark: so more species of insects, birds and mammals can live there / they act as corridors between habitats
questions.explanation: In monoculture farmland, hedgerows add a range of habitats that support many more species.

questions.question: Explain how recycling resources can help to maintain biodiversity.
markScheme: 1 mark: less waste goes to landfill / less land used for landfill and less pollution
1 mark: fewer new raw materials need to be extracted (less quarrying or mining), so fewer habitats are destroyed
questions.explanation: Recycling reduces two pressures on habitats: land used for waste and land used to extract raw materials.

questions.question: Suggest why breeding programmes in zoos are not enough on their own to save an endangered species from extinction.
markScheme: 1 mark: the species needs a safe habitat in the wild to be released into / habitat must also be protected
1 mark: captive populations are small, so genetic variety may be low; or animals bred in captivity may not survive in the wild
questions.explanation: Captive breeding must be combined with habitat protection and careful management of genetic variety.

questions.question: Describe one positive and one negative human interaction in an ecosystem, and explain the impact of each on biodiversity.
markScheme: 1 mark: a named negative interaction, for example deforestation or pollution
1 mark: a named positive interaction, for example a breeding programme or replanting hedgerows
1 mark: correct explanation of the impact on biodiversity for each (habitat loss reduces species; extra habitat or protection maintains or increases species)
questions.explanation: The specification asks students to describe both positive and negative human interactions and explain their impact on biodiversity.

questions.question: A farmer says: 'Leaving field margins costs me money.' Suggest two ways in which leaving field margins could benefit the farmer.
markScheme: 1 mark each, up to 2: more pollinating insects improve pollination of crops; more predators of crop pests, so fewer pests and less pesticide needed; government payments or grants
questions.explanation: Conservation measures can also bring economic benefits to farmers, which helps to resolve the conflict.

questions.question: Describe the programmes that scientists and concerned citizens have put in place to reduce the negative effects of humans on biodiversity.
markScheme: Indicative content: breeding programmes for endangered species (zoos, increase numbers, maintain genetic variety, release into wild); protection and regeneration of rare habitats (nature reserves, marine protected areas, replanting, rewetting bogs); reintroduction of field margins and hedgerows in monoculture farmland (food, shelter, corridors); reduction of deforestation and carbon dioxide emissions by governments (protect forests, renewable energy, slow global warming); recycling rather than landfill (less land used, less pollution, fewer raw materials extracted).
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): at least three programmes described with an explanation of how each helps biodiversity.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two programmes named with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Strong answers name each programme and say how it maintains biodiversity.

questions.question:
A large area of farmland next to a river is used to grow a single crop. A conservation group wants the farmer to plant hedgerows, leave 6 m field margins and stop draining a wet meadow beside the river. The farmer would receive a government payment, but it is less than the income from the crops that would be lost.
Evaluate the conflicting pressures on the farmer and the conservation group, and suggest a solution.
markScheme: Indicative content (benefits for biodiversity): monoculture has low biodiversity; hedgerows and field margins provide food, shelter and nesting sites and act as corridors; more species of insects, birds and mammals; wet meadow is a rare habitat supporting wetland plants, amphibians and birds; regenerating it maintains biodiversity; margins may reduce fertiliser and pesticide run-off into the river.
Benefits for the farmer: more pollinators and natural predators of pests; possible reduction in pesticide use; government payment; improved soil protection.

Costs and pressures: less land for crops, reduced yield and income; payment does not cover losses; cost and time of planting hedgerows; hedgerows need maintenance; demand for food from a growing population.

Possible solutions: narrower margins or margins only on less productive land; higher or additional payments; phased introduction; selling produce as wildlife-friendly; sharing costs with the conservation group.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): balanced evaluation of benefits to biodiversity and costs to the farmer, with detailed biological explanation and a justified, realistic solution.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some benefits and some costs described, with a solution that is not fully justified.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, mostly one-sided.
questions.explanation: The question asks you to evaluate conflicting pressures, so both sides must be weighed and the solution should address the farmer's financial concern while maintaining biodiversity.

questions.question: Which of these is a negative human interaction in an ecosystem?
options: Setting up a marine protected area
Releasing untreated sewage into a river
markScheme: 1 mark: releasing untreated sewage into a river
questions.explanation: Untreated sewage pollutes water and kills organisms, reducing biodiversity. The other options are positive interactions.

questions.question: Name one place where breeding programmes for endangered species are carried out.
markScheme: 1 mark: zoo / wildlife park / conservation centre / botanic garden for plants
questions.explanation: Zoos and conservation centres breed endangered animals; botanic gardens and seed banks protect endangered plants.
